title: House Joint Resolution 6: English as the Official Language

context.text: Placed on the ballot by the Idaho Legislature. HJR 6 passed the House 59-8-3 and the Senate 30-5-0 in March 2025.

question.text: “Shall Article X of the Constitution of the State of Idaho be amended by the addition of a new Section 8, to provide that the English language shall be the official language for the state of Idaho, and to further provide that, except as required by federal law, English shall be used in all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution in the state of Idaho?”

summary.text: The official Statement of Meaning, Purpose, and Result says the amendment “would designate English as the official state language. All official speeches, meetings, and other proceedings of state and local governments, such as city council meetings and jury trials, would be conducted in English, and instruction in public schools would be provided in English. All documents of state and local government entities would be published in English. However, the amendment would allow languages other than English to be used when required by federal law.” The pamphlet text as retrieved does not include a fiscal-impact statement.

measure.yesMeans: A YES vote would designate English the official state language of Idaho.
measure.noMeans: A NO vote would make no change to Idaho’s Constitution, which currently does not designate an official state language.

argumentsFor.text: Official voter pamphlet statement for the amendment: “The amendment could encourage non-English speakers to learn English to be able to better participate in public life. This could promote unity and create a stronger sense of community and shared identity. Non-English speakers would still have language assistance for critical government services, because that is required by federal law.”
Official voter pamphlet statement for the amendment: “The amendment could promote cost-efficient government by limiting the resources spent on communications in languages other than English.”

argumentsAgainst.text: Official voter pamphlet statement against the amendment: “The amendment is unnecessary because state law already makes English the official state language. The existing law is better than the amendment because the existing law is much more detailed. For example, the law allows public schools to teach foreign languages to interested students. The amendment, by requiring that all public instruction be conducted in English, might not allow this.”
Official voter pamphlet statement against the amendment: “The amendment could create social division by signaling to non-English speakers that they are unwelcome in the state and their communities.”

currentLaw.text: The pamphlet says a NO vote “would make no change to Idaho’s Constitution, which currently does not designate an official state language.” The pamphlet's statement against adds that “state law already makes English the official state language”; the Idaho Capital Sun likewise reports that the designation exists in state statute but not in the constitution.

fiscalImpact.text: The resolution's Statement of Purpose/Fiscal Note (prepared by its proponents) says: “There is an estimated cost of up to $300,000 for the Secretary of State to publish proposed constitutional amendments and arguments in a voter's pamphlet as required by law. The costs will occur anyway if any other amendments or ballot initiatives qualify for the November 2026 general election ballot.”

supporters.text: Sen. Brian Lenney (R-Nampa), co-sponsor, and Reps. Dale Hawkins, Kyle Harris and Mike Moyle, co-sponsors (listed on the resolution's Statement of Purpose)

opponents.text: Sen. Melissa Wintrow (D-Boise), Senate Minority Leader, who said putting the amendment on the ballot was a waste of taxpayer dollars
